title: Repository changed Origin and Label, apt-get update fails
body:
## Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
After commit 38ddbef, `apt-get update` fails with message
```
E: Repository 'https://<redacted-host>/ubuntu/jammy jammy InRelease' changed its 'Origin' value from '. jammy' to '<redacted-host>'
E: Repository 'https://<redacted-host>/ubuntu/jammy jammy InRelease' changed its 'Label' value from '. jammy' to 'fluent-bit'
```
**To Reproduce**
- Rubular link if applicable:
- Example log message if applicable:
```
E: Repository 'https://<redacted-host>/ubuntu/jammy jammy InRelease' changed its 'Origin' value from '. jammy' to '<redacted-host>'
E: Repository 'https://<redacted-host>/ubuntu/jammy jammy InRelease' changed its 'Label' value from '. jammy' to 'fluent-bit'

```
- Steps to reproduce the problem:

**Expected behavior**

apt-get update doesn't fail on already added repos

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Hi,

I'm a bit late to the party, but here is what i get right now for Debian bookworm : 

```
$ curl -sSfL https://<redacted-host>/debian/bookworm/dists/bookworm/Release
Origin: . bookworm
Label: . bookworm
Suite: bookworm
Codename: bookworm
Date: Wed, 23 Apr 2025 23:31:13 UTC
Architectures: amd64 arm64
Components: main
Description: Generated by aptly
```

I might be wrong, but it strongly seems that setting `. bookworm` as `Origin` and `Label` is wrong.

Those fields (`Origin` in particular) should describe where the packages are comming from, and `. bookworm` does't serve that purpose.

Is there an issue or PR that show the rationale for this change, and a discussion leading to a decision?

Thanks

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Here is the official documentation for this file format : https://wiki.debian.org/DebianRepository/Format

> These fields are optional. They may be displayed to the user by package management tool or used for pinning. It is suggested that any repository published for other users to use fills meaningful information in these fields so that the user can tell apart different repositories. 

I don't think that `. bookworm` is meaningful information and will help users tell apart different repositories.

comments.author: participant2

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
@participant3 the issue is if we change it then it breaks all current users as they have to explicitly accept the new information. I think we all agree that we should have better information in there but we need a plan or approach for how to roll that out.

This is what we need, not the actual simple change to packaging which we can do quite easily but this was reverted due to the impact on existing users. I will reopen the issue but we need a solution to the underlying problem for existing users.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
@participant2 Hi.

As I understand it, the metadata used to be "correct" (with coherent values, that respect the spirit of the data format), then they have been changed to something subjectively bad, and now we wonder what to do to revert to correct values without breaking people who have the "incorrect" values.
If this is the situation, then I fail to see why we don't simply revert to the correct values and deal with the mistake.
Because right now, all the people who haven't upgraded for some time, there is a breaking change. And everyone accepting the change will have "incorrect" metadata in their local cache.

Maybe I've got all of this wrong in the first place, and that may explain why I see the solution as obvious when you see it as hard.

Also, please note that I use "correct" and "incorrect" adjectives without any judgemental intent, but with the data format specification in mind.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
OK I'm a little confused, my understanding was the following:

1. We have had "incorrect" values for a long time
2. More recently we tried to make them "correct" but this caused an issue for everyone who was already using the existing repos so I reverted: https://github.com/fluent/fluent-bit/issues/10042#issuecomment-2700449580

So the values we have should be the ones we have had for a very long time, i.e. "incorrect". Are we saying this is not true? That is a concern if so and I thought I'd resolved.

Or is it that some folks picked up the "correct" values whilst they were briefly live but now we have reverted for others?

The problem I was explaining was primarily how to make things better without breaking folks stuck with the older incorrect values. That's that main issue I would like to tackle probably more generally - it's likely more of a process/announcement/docs issue unless there is a particular way we can handle it automatically?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Hi @participant2 

I guess it's my fault that we are both confused. I'm sorry about that.
You probably have a better view of the timeline than me.

To clarify, here is what I consider to be "correct" values ✅ :
```
Origin: <redacted-host>
Label: fluent-bit
```
… and "incorrect" values ❌ :
```
Origin: . bookworm
Label: . bookworm
```

Do you agree?

I don't know when/how I picked up incorrect values on some of servers, and I don't think it's important.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Ok yeah that clarifies things and is what I expected. 

Let's call the incorrect ones, what we have now, as v1 and the updated correct ones as v2.

V1 was in place for a very long time, it predates me and the current build & release process.

V2 was something we switched to recently but then it triggered the issue here with everyone on v1 now blocked from updating so we reverted back to v1.

It looks like you picked up the V2 version during this period so you're hitting the same problem but in the opposite direction. 

For me, the question is how should we migrate to V2 without impacting folks and breaking upgrades? The actual technical change is trivial and in the PR we did earlier this year but it causes the problem in this issue. Is there a way we can automate the update to the repo metadata? 

Currently my thinking is the only way we can do it is to create a new endpoint with updated repo metadata whilst keeping the old one. We can then update docs and install scripts to use the new endpoint. 

This should be doable via the current release automation we have, ideally we can serve the updated metadata without having to duplicate the release binaries themselves.

At some future point we can then remove the old repo endpoint with notice to the community.

Or do we just switch and tell folks to update their repo info? This has the most impact for folks and how do we communicate it?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Creating a new endpoint is interresting but it looks like killing an ant with a jackhammer.

Personnaly, if the current metadata would be "correct" and I had "incorrect" ones in cache, I wouldn't mind forcing APT to accept the new data, even if it's annoying.

This doesn't seem to be so hard to do, and too much of a burden.

Managing this via different endpoint, lots of documentation… seems harder, just to fix a temporary mistake.

But this is obviously a subjective opinion and others might see this differently.
